item.text: {"text":"HSTU’s ICML 2024 paper introduces relative position/time attention biases, making content, ordering, and temporal-distance effects relevant diagnostic axes ([HSTU](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17152v3)). *Measuring Recency Bias* (2024) proposes quantifying excessive dependence on recent interactions and reports performance improvements from mitigation; recency sensitivity alone therefore does not establish useful relevance ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722)). SIGIR 2026’s *Diagnosing and Mitigating Mid-Sequence Degradation* reports boundary-focused sensitivity persisting when informative collaborative signals are relocated, supporting controlled relocation experiments; its findings do not establish the same behavior in HSTU ([paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805712.3809738)).\n\nSuggested synthesis for one frozen HSTU: compare equal-size recent versus older content replacements while preserving occupied slots, timestamps, sequence length, and the final readout event; separately shuffle earlier events while preserving their item multiset and final event. Deletion alone confounds content removal with position changes. To isolate absolute-position sensitivity, shift explicit position IDs while preserving content, relative distances, timestamps, masks, and readout identity, where the architecture permits; moving events instead also changes causal context. Always read the final nonpadding position in left-padded histories. Use identical candidates for paired target-rank changes, top-10 entry/exit rates, and user-bootstrap uncertainty. Include identity transformations, edits to fully masked padding, and matched random replacements as controls; distinguish fixed timestamp slots from timestamps traveling with events. Older-history replacement improving validation ranks suggests harmful historical dependence under that intervention, not observed user intent. These are proposed model-sensitivity probes, not an established HSTU causal-identification procedure."}
